name: Tulum & the Riviera Maya
tagline: White sand, turquoise water and a small Maya fortress on a cliff above the Caribbean, with jungle cenotes and the world's second-largest barrier reef offshore.
highlight: The Tulum ruins above the sea in the early morning, followed by a swim in a jungle cenote.
shortDescription: Mexico's Caribbean coast south of Cancún: Tulum's cliff-top Maya ruins and beach, Cobá's jungle pyramid, swimmable cenotes, snorkelling with turtles and laid-back beach towns.
metaDescription: A Tulum and Riviera Maya travel guide: the Tulum ruins, Cobá, cenotes, Akumal turtles and Sian Ka'an, beaches, Playa del Carmen, sargassum season, where to stay and a three-day plan.
nearestAirport: Cancún International (CUN), about 1 hour 30 minutes; Tulum International (TQO) is now open
knownFor: The Tulum ruins, cenotes, beaches, snorkelling, Sian Ka'an
goodFor: Beaches, snorkelling, cenotes, Maya ruins, relaxing

image.file: File:Tulum - God of the Winds Temple 04.JPG
image.alt: The Temple of the God of the Winds at Tulum, on a cliff above the Caribbean

intro: The Caribbean coast of the Yucatán, known as the Riviera Maya, runs about 130 km from Cancún south to Tulum, a string of beaches, coves, lagoons and small resort towns backed by jungle. Offshore lies the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef, the second-largest in the world. Before the Spanish arrived, the coast was a busy Maya trading route, and its ruins are dotted along the shore.

Tulum, the Maya walled city, is the most photographed: a small but beautifully sited fortress of temples on a limestone cliff, with a white beach below. It was an important port between about 1200 and 1500 CE and was still occupied when the Spanish arrived. Nearby, Cobá is a much larger city in the jungle with a pyramid you can climb, and the Sian Ka'an biosphere reserve protects mangroves, lagoons and reef.

Development has been intense, and Tulum in particular has changed from a hippie hideaway to a fashionable, expensive resort strip. It still offers wonderful swimming, cenotes and easy access to the Maya world, and quieter alternatives exist in Akumal, Bacalar and Sian Ka'an. Sargassum seaweed can affect the beaches in some seasons.

whyVisit.intro: Tulum and the Riviera Maya combine beaches, snorkelling, cenotes and ruins within a short drive.

points.title: Ruins above the sea
points.text: Tulum's temples stand on a cliff, with the Caribbean turquoise behind, one of the most striking settings for any ancient site.

points.title: Cenotes
points.text: Dozens of sinkholes, from open pools to caves with stalactites, are within a short drive.

points.title: Snorkelling and diving
points.text: Sea turtles graze at Akumal, and the reef offers snorkelling, scuba and freediving.

points.title: Cobá
points.text: A large jungle city with sacbé roads, stelae and the tallest pyramid in the northern Yucatán.

points.title: Nature reserves
points.text: Sian Ka'an and the lagoon of Bacalar offer wildlife, kayaking and quiet.

attractionsIntro: The ruins take half a day, and the beaches, cenotes and reserve fill the rest.

attractions.name: The Tulum ruins

image.file: File:Stairs to the Caribbean - Tulum Maya site, QR.jpg
image.alt: Stairs leading down to the Caribbean beach beside the Tulum Maya site

attractions.text: A walled Maya city of about 60 buildings on a cliff, including El Castillo, the Temple of the Frescoes and the Temple of the Descending God. A small beach lies below.
attractions.tip: Go at opening or late afternoon, and swim from the beach.

attractions.name: Cobá

image.file: File:Nohoch Mul Pyramid 2 - Cobá Maya site QR 2020.jpg
image.alt: The Nohoch Mul pyramid at the Maya site of Cobá in the jungle

attractions.text: A jungle city spread over lakes, linked by raised stone roads, with the 42-metre Nohoch Mul pyramid, the highest in the region. Bikes and pedicabs are available inside.
attractions.tip: Rent a bike at the entrance. Check whether climbing is permitted.

attractions.name: Gran Cenote and Dos Ojos
attractions.text: Two of the most popular cenotes, with crystal-clear water, stalactites and cave diving and snorkelling routes.
attractions.tip: Go early, before the tour groups.

attractions.name: Akumal Bay
attractions.text: A sheltered bay where green sea turtles graze on seagrass, easily seen while snorkelling. Regulations require a guide and a life jacket.
attractions.tip: Follow the rules and do not touch the turtles.

attractions.name: Sian Ka'an Biosphere Reserve
attractions.text: A UNESCO reserve of about 5,000 km² of mangroves, lagoons, jungle and reef south of Tulum, with dolphins, manatees, crocodiles and over 300 bird species.

attractions.name: Playa del Carmen and Cozumel
attractions.text: A lively resort town with a pedestrian Fifth Avenue, and a ferry to Cozumel, an island with excellent diving.
attractions.tip: Use Playa as a transport hub.

thingsToDoIntro: The Riviera Maya is built around sun, sea and short excursions.

thingsToDo.title: Visit Tulum at opening
thingsToDo.text: Explore the ruins in cool light, then swim at the small beach below.

thingsToDo.title: Swim in a cenote
thingsToDo.text: Try the Gran Cenote, Dos Ojos, Cenote Calavera or Casa Cenote.
thingsToDo.tip: Bring reef-safe sunscreen and rinse first.

thingsToDo.title: Snorkel with turtles at Akumal
thingsToDo.text: Green turtles swim in the shallows of the bay.

thingsToDo.title: Rent a bike at Cobá
thingsToDo.text: Ride through the jungle between temples, and climb the pyramid if allowed.

thingsToDo.title: Kayak at Bacalar
thingsToDo.text: The Lagoon of Seven Colours, two hours south, has clear water in many blues, stromatolites and kayaks.

thingsToDo.title: Relax on a beach
thingsToDo.text: Beaches from Playa del Carmen to Tulum offer white sand and clear water, though sargassum can affect them in spring and summer.

foodIntro: The coast serves Yucatecan classics and fresh seafood, along with a growing international food scene.

foods.name: Ceviche and fresh seafood
foods.text: Raw fish cured in lime with onion, tomato and coriander, and grilled catch of the day.

foods.name: Cochinita pibil and tacos
foods.text: Yucatecan pork and grilled fish tacos, sold in taquerías in Tulum town.

foods.name: Fresh coconut and fruit
foods.text: Coconut water and sliced mango or papaya with chile and lime.

foods.name: Lionfish
foods.text: An invasive species that is now hunted and served on menus. It has a mild, sweet flavour.

foods.name: Craft cocktails and mezcal
foods.text: Cocktail bars and beach clubs pour mezcal margaritas.

foods.name: Guacamole and tortillas
foods.text: Made to order at the table.

accommodation.intro: Choose between Tulum town (cheaper, walkable), the beach road (pricey, atmospheric) and the quieter smaller towns.

areas.name: Tulum town
areas.text: Guesthouses, hostels and small hotels with restaurants and tour operators.

areas.name: The Tulum beach road
areas.text: Boutique hotels and eco-lodges along the sand, expensive and often lacking mains power and water.

areas.name: Akumal, Bacalar and Sian Ka'an
areas.text: Smaller places away from the crowds.

gettingThere.intro: Tulum is about 130 km south of Cancún.

options.text: The main gateway, with buses and shuttles running to Tulum in about 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours.
A new airport near Tulum with a growing number of flights.
ADO buses run along the coast, and the Tren Maya connects Cancún with Tulum.

gettingAround.intro: Colectivos, taxis and hire cars link the towns, and bicycles are common in Tulum.

options.text: Shared vans run along Highway 307 between Playa del Carmen and Tulum, cheaply.
Taxis in Tulum are expensive, particularly along the beach road. Agree the fare.
options.detail: Uber is restricted in some places.

options.text: A car gives freedom to reach cenotes and Cobá, and bikes are useful in town and on the beach road.
options.detail: Watch for police checkpoints and speed bumps.

bestTime.headline: November–April
bestTime.summary: The dry winter and spring are the best time. Summer is hot and rainy, sargassum is worse from April to August, and hurricanes can occur from June to November.

seasons.text: Warm, sunny and dry, with clear water. The high season.
Hot, with increasing sargassum on some beaches.
Hot, humid and rainy, with hurricane risk and sargassum. Low prices.
Peak hurricane risk in October. Improving by late November.

bestTime.avoid: Hurricane season, and Christmas and Easter for crowds.

itinerary.title: Three days in Tulum
itinerary.intro: The ruins and beach on the first day, cenotes and Cobá on the second, Akumal and Sian Ka'an on the third.

days.title: Tulum ruins and beach
days.afternoon: A swim and lunch on the beach.

days.title: Turtles and reserve
days.afternoon: A boat trip in Sian Ka'an.

tipsIntro: Tulum is popular, and a few tips help.
tips: Go to Tulum and Cobá early, before the heat and the tour groups.
Use reef-safe sunscreen, and rinse off before entering cenotes.
Check sargassum reports and hurricane forecasts before you book.
Carry pesos. Many restaurants in Tulum quote in dollars at poor rates.
Book beach hotels and restaurants ahead in winter.
Follow rules on turtles, reefs and protected areas.

faq.a: Yes, for the ruins, beaches and cenotes, though it has become expensive and crowded. Quieter alternatives include Akumal, Bacalar and Sian Ka'an.
It can be from April to August, with some beaches covered in seaweed. Conditions vary by week and beach, so check reports.

faq.q: Can I climb the pyramid at Cobá?
faq.a: Climbing has been restricted in recent years. Check the current rules at the entrance.

faq.q: How many days do you need?
faq.a: Three or four for Tulum, Cobá and cenotes. A week lets you add Bacalar and Sian Ka'an.

faq.q: How far is Tulum from Cancún?
faq.a: About 130 km, or 1.5 to 2 hours by road.
It is heavily visited, and most visits are trouble-free. Petty crime and occasional violence occur, so check your government's advice and use common sense.
